chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
title: Why today's players lack the old musicians' versatility
summary: Jackson blames disc jockeys, booking agents and a trend away from big bands, though young people now ask where the music came from.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: I would like to ask you just right now, just to interject this. What do you attribute to that the young black musicians don't have -- we have this era of all these instrumentalists like Bennie Carter and Chick Webb and Don Redmon and Garvin Bushell and Sam Wooding that played all of these great, all these instruments, these academic instruments like the flute and piccolo and bassoon -- and in this era we don't have too much of that.

I attribute that to disc jockeys, to our booking agents, to the trend of music that they are putting in front of these people. There's not music, actually, that you can learn anything from. There's no more big bands where that you can learn to play with a section. Everything is so individualistic now, you see. And everybody, if you listen, they all sound the same. They sound the same. You can make a million dollars on one record and a guitar player can learn five chords and get rich.
That's absolutely so, but I find that --

But now they want to know. The kids want to know now. Now they want to know now. They're going through a nostalgic era right now. And if you play colleges and you go around and do clinics and things, they want to know why, where did this come from, you see.
